Battle of Monte Cassino. The Battle of Monte Cassino was a four-month campaign from January to May 1944 by Allied forces to capture the strategic height dominating the Gustav Line, Germany's main defensive position in central Italy. The hilltop monastery became the symbol of bitter, grinding mountain warfare. Monks were evacuated, the ancient monastery was controversially bombed, and wave after wave of assaults by Polish, New Zealand, French, and American forces failed against entrenched German paratroopers. A Polish force finally captured the ruined monastery on May 18, 1944, breaking the Gustav Line and opening the road to Rome. Monte Cassino exemplified the brutal, attritional nature of the Italian campaign.

The Gustav Line stretched across Italy from the Tyrrhenian to the Ionian Sea, anchored on the strategic height of Monte Cassino at seventeen hundred feet. German General Albert Kesselring made it his primary defensive position. The mountain overlooked the Liri Valley and the route to Rome, fortified with bunkers, barbed wire, and minefields with German paratroopers and elite infantry garrisoning the position. The sixth-century Benedictine monastery atop the mountain held both spiritual and strategic significance, with Allied commanders debating whether it contained German observers.

The first attack from January 17 to February 12 saw American II Corps attack up the mountain, suffering two thousand casualties, and being repulsed. A controversial bombing of the monastery by two hundred twenty-nine bombers followed from February 15 to 18, with many Allies and historians debating whether it was necessary or desirable. The third attack from March 15 to 23 brought another bombing campaign and assault by the Eighth Army, but German defenses held. The fourth attack from May 11 to 18 saw a coordinated offensive by American, British, French, Polish, and Canadian forces finally break through. Polish II Corps captured the monastery ruins on May 18.

The German line collapsed after May 18 as Kesselring ordered withdrawal northward to the Hitler Line and ultimately to the Gothic Line. Allied forces liberated Rome on June 4, 1944. Momentum up the peninsula accelerated, though German defensive skill meant the war in Italy continued until 1945. For Allied forces, the battle illustrated that mountain terrain, entrenchment, and German skill could negate numerical superiority.
